lessons.title: Life cycle assessment and recycling
lessons.summary: Learn how to extract copper from low-grade ores using plants and bacteria, how a life cycle assessment measures the environmental impact of a product from cradle to grave, and why reducing, reusing and recycling matter.
objectives: I can describe phytomining and bioleaching as ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores.
I can describe the four stages of a life cycle assessment (LCA).
I can use LCA data to compare the environmental impact of two products.
I can explain why some LCA judgements are difficult to make objectively.
I can explain how recycling metals and glass reduces the use of resources and energy.

activities.title: Copper from low-grade ores
activities.content:
## Running out of the easy copper

Copper is used in wiring, plumbing and electronics, and demand keeps rising. The **high-grade ores**, rocks rich in copper, are nearly used up. What remains are **low-grade ores** with only a tiny percentage of copper, plus huge amounts of waste rock. Traditional mining and smelting of these would be **expensive** and produce vast spoil heaps and sulfur dioxide.

Two new biological methods extract copper from low-grade ores and even from mining waste.

### Phytomining

1. **Plants** are grown on soil or low-grade ore that contains copper compounds.
2. The plants **absorb** copper compounds through their roots and concentrate them in their leaves and shoots.
3. The plants are **harvested and burned**.
4. The **ash** contains copper compounds, which are dissolved in acid to make a copper solution.

### Bioleaching

1. **Bacteria** are mixed with the low-grade ore.
2. The bacteria feed on the ore and produce a solution containing copper compounds, called a **leachate**.

### Getting the copper out of the solution

Both methods give a **solution of copper ions**. The metal is obtained by either:

- **Electrolysis** of the solution, with copper collecting at the cathode, or
- **Displacement** using scrap iron, which is more reactive than copper: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.

### Pros and cons

These methods avoid the digging, moving and heating of tons of rock, so they use less energy and cause less damage. But they are **slow**: bioleaching can take years, and plants need a growing season.

question.text: Put the stages of phytomining in the correct order.
question.hint: Plants must grow before they can be harvested, and burning comes before the ash can be used.
question.explanation: Grow plants on the ore, let them absorb copper compounds, harvest and burn them, dissolve the ash in acid, then extract copper from the solution by electrolysis or displacement.
order: Grow plants on soil containing copper compounds
The plants absorb copper compounds into their tissues
Dissolve the ash in acid to make a copper solution
Extract copper by electrolysis or displacement with scrap iron

activities.title: Worked example: choosing an extraction method
activities.content:
**A mining company owns a site containing 0.3% copper. Compare traditional mining with bioleaching for this site.**

**Traditional mining and smelting**

- Would need to dig up and crush over 300 tonnes of rock for every tonne of copper.
- Smelting needs high temperatures, so a lot of **energy** and carbon dioxide.
- Copper sulfide ores release **sulfur dioxide** when heated, causing acid rain.
- Fast and well understood, but **not economic** for such a low-grade ore.

**Bioleaching**

- Bacteria produce a copper leachate with **no digging, crushing or smelting**, so far less energy and no sulfur dioxide.
- Works on ore that is too poor for traditional methods, and even on old spoil heaps.
- Much **slower**: it could take years to produce the same amount of copper.
- The leachate is **toxic** and must be contained so it does not pollute groundwater.

**Judgement:** for a 0.3% ore, bioleaching is the only option that makes sense economically and environmentally, provided the company can wait for the copper and manage the leachate safely.

The pattern for evaluate questions again: an advantage and a disadvantage of each, then a decision with a reason.

question.text: Which statements about bioleaching are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what does the work, how fast it is, and what the product looks like.
question.explanation: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce a solution of copper compounds (leachate) from which copper is obtained by displacement or electrolysis. It is slow, not fast, and it avoids the high temperatures of smelting.

options.text: Bacteria produce a solution containing copper compounds.
Copper can be obtained from the leachate by adding scrap iron.
It is much faster than traditional smelting.
options.feedback: Bioleaching is slow and can take years.

options.text: It requires the ore to be heated to a high temperature.
options.feedback: No smelting is needed, which is one of its advantages.

activities.title: Life cycle assessment
activities.content:
## From cradle to grave

A **life cycle assessment (LCA)** works out the **environmental impact** of a product over its **whole life**, not just when it is used. There are four stages to consider.

### 1. Extracting and processing raw materials

Mining metal ores, drilling for oil, growing crops or cutting timber. This uses energy, may damage habitats and creates waste.

### 2. Manufacturing and packaging

Turning raw materials into the product. Energy use, water use, waste and pollution from the factory, plus the packaging the product is sold in.

### 3. Use and operation during its lifetime

Some products have almost no impact in use (a glass bottle); others use energy or produce waste for years (a car, a washing machine). Products that last longer usually have a lower impact per year.

### 4. Disposal at the end of its useful life

Landfill takes up space and may release methane or leach chemicals. Incineration releases carbon dioxide and possibly toxic gases. **Recycling** reduces the impact.

### What is measured

At each stage, an LCA looks at:

- **energy** used
- **water** used
- **raw materials** consumed
- **waste** and **pollutants** produced

The results are compared with those for an alternative product, so that companies or governments can choose the option with the lower overall impact.

Transport between stages counts too: a product shipped halfway round the world has a bigger footprint than the same product made locally.

activities.title: Worked example: plastic bag or paper bag?
activities.content:
**Use the LCA data to compare a plastic (poly(ethene)) bag with a paper bag.**

| Stage | Plastic bag | Paper bag |
|---|---|---|
| raw materials | crude oil (finite) | timber (renewable, but forestry uses land) |
| manufacturing | fractional distillation, cracking, polymerisation: moderate energy | pulping and bleaching: high energy and lots of water |
| use | strong, light, can be reused many times | weak when wet, usually single use |
| disposal | not biodegradable; litter; can be recycled | biodegradable; easily recycled |

**Analysis**

- The plastic bag uses a **finite** resource and is a **litter** problem, but it takes **less energy and water** to make and can be **reused**.
- The paper bag is from a **renewable** resource and **rots away**, but making it uses **more energy and water**, and it is heavier so more fuel is used transporting it.

**Conclusion**

Per bag, the plastic bag often has the **lower** total environmental impact, as long as it is reused several times and disposed of properly. The paper bag wins only on disposal and litter. This surprises many people, which is exactly why LCAs are done: intuition is not enough.

**The exam skill:** use the data given, quote it, and reach a balanced conclusion.

question.text: Match each activity to the stage of a life cycle assessment it belongs to.
question.hint: Follow the product from the ground to the bin.
question.explanation: Mining ore is raw material extraction; moulding and boxing is manufacturing and packaging; electricity used while running is the use stage; sending it to landfill is disposal.

pairs.left: moulding the casing and putting it in a box
electricity used by a kettle over 5 years
sending a broken toaster to landfill

activities.title: The limits of an LCA
activities.content:
## Not everything is a number

Some parts of an LCA are easy to measure objectively: the **mass of raw material**, the **energy in kilowatt-hours**, the **litres of water**. Other parts are much harder.

### The difficult judgements

- **Pollutant effects**: how do you compare a tonne of carbon dioxide with a kilogram of a toxic metal in a river? Each harms the environment in a different way, so putting a single number on them involves **value judgements**.
- **Habitat loss** and effects on wildlife are hard to quantify.
- **Future disposal**: nobody knows exactly how a product will be disposed of in 20 years.

Because of this, two LCAs of the same product by different people can reach **different conclusions**.

### Bias and misuse

An LCA can be **selective**. A company might carry out a shortened or biased LCA that leaves out the stages where its product does badly, then use the result in **advertising** to claim its product is greener. When you read an LCA, ask:

- Who paid for it?
- Were all four stages included?
- Was it checked independently (peer reviewed)?

Exam questions often ask why LCAs are not completely objective, and the answer is the value judgements about pollutants and the possibility of selective use of data.

question.text: Why can two life cycle assessments of the same product reach different conclusions?
question.hint: Some measurements are objective; some parts need opinions.
question.explanation: Numerical values such as energy and water use are objective, but judging how harmful different pollutants are involves value judgements, and assessors may choose to include or leave out different stages or data.

options.text: Comparing the effects of different pollutants involves value judgements, and data may be used selectively.
Energy use cannot be measured.
options.feedback: Energy use is one of the easiest things to measure objectively.

options.text: LCAs only ever look at the use stage.
Products change chemically while being assessed.

activities.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle
activities.content:
## Making resources last

Finite resources will not last for ever, and extracting them causes damage. Three approaches help, in order of preference.

### Reduce

Use less in the first place: thinner cans, less packaging, buying less.

### Reuse

Use the same item again without reprocessing: refillable glass bottles, second-hand clothes. This saves almost all of the energy of making a new item.

### Recycle

Collect the used material and process it into new products.

**Metals** are collected, sorted, melted and recast. Recycling **aluminium** uses only about **5%** of the energy needed to extract it from bauxite by electrolysis. Recycling **steel** saves energy too, and scrap iron can be added to the blast furnace along with new iron ore.

**Glass** is sorted by colour, crushed, melted and reshaped into new bottles and jars. It can be recycled again and again with no loss of quality.

**Plastics** can be melted and remoulded, but different polymers must be sorted first, and quality can drop each time.

### Why recycling matters

- **Conserves finite resources**: less ore mined, less oil extracted.
- **Saves energy**, which usually means less carbon dioxide.
- **Less waste to landfill**.
- **Less environmental damage** from mining and quarrying.

The drawbacks are the cost and energy of collection, sorting and transport, and the fact that some materials cannot be recycled indefinitely. Even so, recycling almost always comes out ahead in an LCA.

question.text: Extracting 1 tonne of aluminium from its ore uses about 15 000 kWh of energy. Recycling aluminium uses about 5% of this. Calculate the energy saved, in kWh, by recycling 1 tonne of aluminium instead of extracting it.
question.hint: Recycling uses 5%, so the saving is 95% of 15 000.
question.explanation: Energy for recycling = 0.05 × 15 000 = 750 kWh. Saving = 15 000 − 750 = 14 250 kWh.

metadata.blanksText: Glass bottles are sorted by colour, crushed and then ___ so they can be reshaped. Metals are recycled by melting and ___ into new products. Recycling reduces the amount of ___ resources that need to be extracted.

question.hint: Both glass and metal need heat. The last word describes resources that will run out.
question.explanation: Glass is melted, metals are melted and recast, and recycling conserves finite resources.

question.text:
A company carries out a life cycle assessment to compare drinks containers made from aluminium and from glass. Some of the data are shown.

| | Aluminium can | Glass bottle |
|---|---|---|
| raw material | bauxite ore | sand, limestone, sodium carbonate |
| energy to make one container | high (electrolysis) | moderate (furnace) |
| mass of container | 15 g | 200 g |
| recycling | can be recycled repeatedly, uses 5% of extraction energy | can be recycled repeatedly |

(a) State the four stages considered in a life cycle assessment.

(b) Using the data, give one advantage of the aluminium can and one advantage of the glass bottle.

(c) Explain why recycling aluminium cans is so beneficial compared with making new ones.

(d) Suggest why the company's LCA might not be completely reliable.
question.hint: Four stages from raw materials to disposal. Think about mass and transport. Electrolysis uses a lot of energy. Value judgements and bias.
question.explanation: (a) Extracting raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use; disposal. (b) The can is much lighter (15 g vs 200 g) so less fuel is used in transport; the glass bottle needs less energy to make and uses abundant raw materials. (c) Extracting aluminium by electrolysis uses a large amount of energy; recycling uses only about 5% of that, saving energy, reducing carbon dioxide emissions and conserving bauxite. (d) Some judgements about the impact of pollutants are subjective, and the company may have selected data that favours its own product.

markScheme.criterion: Four stages: raw materials, manufacturing/packaging, use, disposal
Advantage of aluminium can: lighter so less energy for transport / recycling saves 95% of energy
Advantage of glass: less energy to manufacture / raw materials abundant / can be reused
Extraction of aluminium by electrolysis needs a large amount of energy
Recycling uses only ~5% of the energy, so saves energy / reduces CO₂ / conserves bauxite
LCA involves value judgements about pollutants / company may be biased or use data selectively

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Low-grade copper ores** can be worked by **phytomining** (plants absorb copper compounds, are burned, ash dissolved) and **bioleaching** (bacteria produce a copper leachate). Copper is recovered by **electrolysis** or **displacement with scrap iron**. Both are slow but low energy.
- **Life cycle assessment (LCA)** measures environmental impact over four stages: **raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal**, looking at energy, water, resources and waste.
- Some parts of an LCA (energy, water) are objective; **judging pollutant effects involves value judgements**, and LCAs can be **misused selectively** in advertising.
- **Reduce, reuse, recycle** conserves finite resources, saves energy and cuts waste. Recycling aluminium uses about **5%** of the extraction energy; glass and metals are melted and reformed.

practiceQuestions.text: Which method of copper extraction uses plants?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Phytomining grows plants that absorb copper compounds; bioleaching uses bacteria.

options.text: phytomining
bioleaching
smelting
electrolysis

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a life cycle assessment only considers the environmental impact of a product while it is being used.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. An LCA covers raw material extraction, manufacturing, use and disposal.

options.text: True

practiceQuestions.hint: Tiny living organisms; the name of the solution begins with the same letters as 'leach'.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bacteria produce a leachate containing copper compounds.

practiceQuestions.text: Scrap iron is added to a solution of copper sulfate obtained by bioleaching. What happens?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the reactivity of iron and copper.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.

options.text: Iron displaces copper, which forms as a solid.
Copper displaces iron from the solution.
options.feedback: Copper is less reactive than iron.

options.text: Nothing happens because iron is unreactive.
Hydrogen gas is produced.

practiceQuestions.text: Scrap iron displaces copper from a leachate: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Calculate the mass of copper, in grams, obtained from 5.6 g of iron. (Ar: Fe = 56, Cu = 64)
practiceQuestions.hint: Moles of iron = 5.6 ÷ 56; the ratio is 1 : 1.
practiceQuestions.explanation: moles Fe = 0.1 mol, so 0.1 mol Cu. mass = 0.1 × 64 = 6.4 g.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each term to its meaning.
practiceQuestions.hint: One avoids using, one uses again, one reprocesses.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reduce means using less; reuse means using the same item again; recycle means reprocessing the material into a new product.

pairs.right: use less material in the first place
use the same item again without reprocessing
reprocess the material into new products

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these are benefits of recycling metals? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about ores, energy and waste.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recycling conserves finite metal ores and uses less energy than extraction. It does not create new metal ore, and although it reduces the need for mining it does not eliminate all environmental impact.

options.text: Less metal ore needs to be mined.
Less energy is used than extracting metal from ore.
It creates new deposits of metal ore.
It has no environmental impact at all.
options.feedback: Collection, sorting and melting still use energy.

practiceQuestions.text: A low-grade ore contains 0.4% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of ore, in tonnes, that must be processed to obtain 2 tonnes of copper.
Explain why phytomining and bioleaching are becoming more important, and give one disadvantage of these methods.
practiceQuestions.hint: What is happening to high-grade ores? How long do these methods take?
practiceQuestions.explanation: High-grade copper ores are running out, and demand for copper is rising. Phytomining and bioleaching can extract copper from low-grade ores and waste that would be uneconomic to mine traditionally, using less energy. The main disadvantage is that they are very slow.

markScheme.criterion: High-grade ores are running out / becoming scarce while demand is high
These methods can extract copper from low-grade ores / waste that traditional methods cannot use economically (with less energy)
Disadvantage: slow / toxic leachate / land needed

practiceQuestions.text:
A supermarket wants to decide whether to sell milk in plastic bottles or in cartons made from paper with a thin plastic lining.

(a) Describe the information that would be needed to carry out a life cycle assessment of the two containers.

(b) Explain why the disposal stage is more of a problem for the carton than for the plastic bottle.

(c) Explain why the supermarket should be cautious about using an LCA produced by the carton manufacturer.
practiceQuestions.hint: Energy, water, materials, waste at each stage. Mixed materials are hard to separate. Bias.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) For each stage (raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal): the energy used, water used, raw materials consumed and waste or pollutants produced, including transport. (b) The carton is made of two materials bonded together, so it is difficult to separate and recycle, whereas the plastic bottle is a single polymer that can be recycled easily. (c) The manufacturer may have used data selectively or made value judgements that favour its own product, so the LCA could be biased.

markScheme.criterion: Data on energy, water, raw materials and waste/pollutants produced
At each stage: raw materials, manufacturing, use and disposal (including transport)
Carton is made of mixed materials that are hard to separate so difficult to recycle
Manufacturer's LCA may be biased / selective / not independently checked

practiceQuestions.text: Put the stages of bioleaching in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: The bacteria have to produce the solution before anything can be extracted from it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bacteria are added to the low-grade ore or spoil heap; they produce a solution of copper compounds called a leachate; the leachate is collected; copper is then extracted from it by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
order: Bacteria are added to low-grade copper ore or mine waste
The bacteria produce a solution of copper compounds (leachate)
The leachate is collected from the bottom of the heap
Copper is extracted from the leachate using scrap iron or electrolysis

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements about phytomining are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how the copper gets into the plants and what has to be done to the plants afterwards.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In phytomining, plants absorb copper compounds from the soil through their roots; the plants are harvested and burned, and the ash contains copper compounds that can be dissolved in acid. It is slow and is used for low-grade ores, and the copper is not obtained directly from the leaves as metal.

options.text: The plants absorb copper compounds from the soil through their roots.
The plants are burned and the ash contains copper compounds.
It is a fast way of extracting copper from high-grade ores.
options.feedback: Phytomining is slow and is used for low-grade ores that are not worth mining.

options.text: Pure copper metal is collected directly from the leaves.
options.feedback: The ash must be dissolved in acid and the copper then extracted by electrolysis or displacement.

practiceQuestions.text: A company carries out a life cycle assessment of a cotton T-shirt. Match each activity to the stage of the assessment it belongs to.
practiceQuestions.hint: Follow the T-shirt from the field to the bin.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Growing and picking the cotton is obtaining raw materials; spinning, weaving, dyeing and wrapping is manufacturing and packaging; washing and drying during its life is the use stage; incineration is disposal.

pairs.left: spinning, weaving and dyeing the fabric, then wrapping it
washing and tumble-drying the T-shirt over several years
sending the worn-out T-shirt to be incinerated

practiceQuestions.text: Which part of a life cycle assessment is the most difficult to measure objectively?
practiceQuestions.hint: Numbers such as masses and volumes can be measured; comparing different kinds of harm needs an opinion.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The masses of raw materials, the energy used and the water used can all be measured. Deciding how harmful one pollutant is compared with another involves value judgements, which is why different assessors can reach different conclusions.

options.text: Deciding how much harm different pollutants cause compared with each other
Measuring the mass of raw materials used
Measuring the energy used during manufacture
options.feedback: Energy use can be metered directly.

options.text: Measuring the volume of water used

practiceQuestions.text: Extracting 1 tonne of copper from its ore uses about 9500 kWh of energy. Recycling scrap copper uses about 15% of this. Calculate the energy saved, in kWh, by recycling 1 tonne of copper instead of extracting it from ore.
practiceQuestions.hint: Recycling uses 15%, so the saving is 85% of 9500.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Energy for recycling = 0.15 × 9500 = 1425 kWh. Saving = 9500 − 1425 = 8075 kWh.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about recycling metals.

metadata.blanksText: Scrap metals such as aluminium cans are recycled by ___ them and casting the liquid metal into new products. Recycling uses far less ___ than extracting the metal from its ore, and it reduces the amount of waste that is sent to ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Heat turns the scrap into a liquid. Extraction by electrolysis needs a lot of something. Waste that is buried goes to a particular kind of site.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The scrap is melted and recast; this uses much less energy than extracting metal from ore, and keeps the metal out of landfill.

practiceQuestions.text:
A supermarket carries out a life cycle assessment to compare plastic carrier bags with paper carrier bags. Some of the data are shown.

| | Plastic bag | Paper bag |
|---|---|---|
| raw material | crude oil | trees |
| energy to make one bag | low | higher |
| mass of bag | 6 g | 55 g |
| reuse | can be reused many times | tears easily when wet |
| disposal | not biodegradable | biodegradable |

(a) State the four stages considered in a life cycle assessment.

(b) Using the data, give one advantage of the plastic bag and one advantage of the paper bag.

(c) Explain why the number of times a bag is reused affects the result of the assessment.

(d) Explain why an assessment carried out by a plastic bag manufacturer might reach a different conclusion from one carried out by an environmental group.
practiceQuestions.hint: Raw materials to disposal. Think about mass, energy and what happens in landfill. Reuse means fewer bags are made. Opinions and choice of data.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use during its lifetime; disposal at end of life. (b) The plastic bag is much lighter (6 g against 55 g) so less energy is used to make and transport it, and it can be reused many times; the paper bag is made from a renewable raw material and is biodegradable. (c) A bag that is reused many times replaces many single-use bags, so the impact of making it is spread over more uses and fewer bags need to be manufactured and disposed of. (d) Comparing the harm caused by different pollutants involves value judgements, and each organisation may select the data or stages that favour the conclusion it wants.

markScheme.criterion: Four stages: raw materials, manufacturing/packaging, use, disposal
Advantage of plastic: lighter / less energy to make / can be reused
Advantage of paper: renewable raw material / biodegradable
Reuse means fewer bags need to be made / impact spread over more uses
Comparing pollutants involves value judgements / is subjective
Data or stages may be chosen selectively / bias towards a desired conclusion
